title: Indonesian Stocks Plunge to Six‑Year Low Amid Rising MSCI Downgrade Fears
body:
Indonesia’s main equity gauge slumped more than 5 percent on Monday, sinking to its lowest point since 2018 as investors braced for a possible downgrade of the country’s market classification by MSCI. The sharp sell‑off sparked fears that foreign capital could flee the archipelago’s bourses, putting additional pressure on a market already rattled by a slowdown in global growth and volatile commodity prices.

The Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) closed at 5,882 points, a level not seen since the end of 2018, after a steep decline that began early in the session. Trading volumes surged, with foreign investors offloading roughly $1.2 billion worth of shares, according to data from the Indonesia Stock Exchange. Domestic investors also sold, but the bulk of the pressure came from overseas funds that had been net buyers earlier in the year. The index’s tumble erased much of the modest gains recorded in the first half of 2024 and widened the gap between Indonesia and its regional peers, such as Malaysia and Thailand, whose markets remained relatively stable.

The catalyst behind the panic is MSCI’s ongoing review of its Emerging Markets (EM) classification, which could see Indonesia moved from the EM to the Frontier Markets (FM) category. A downgrade would mean that many passive funds tracking MSCI’s EM indices would be forced to sell Indonesian equities to remain compliant, potentially withdrawing an estimated $30 billion in assets under management. While MSCI has not yet announced a final decision, its interim findings highlighted concerns over Indonesia’s market depth, liquidity and corporate governance standards—issues that have lingered despite reforms introduced after the 2018 financial turbulence.

Analysts warn that the mere prospect of a downgrade can be as destabilising as an actual reclassification. “Investors are pricing in a worst‑case scenario,” said Rina Suryani, senior equity strategist at Mandiri Sekuritas. “Even if MSCI ultimately keeps Indonesia in the EM basket, the market reaction has already inflicted a significant hit to confidence, which could linger for months.” The sentiment is echoed by foreign fund managers who cite the need for greater transparency in corporate disclosures and a more robust regulatory framework to safeguard minority shareholders. Some have already begun reallocating capital to other Southeast Asian markets that offer higher liquidity and lower perceived risk.

The broader macro environment adds another layer of uncertainty. Indonesia’s economy, the largest in ASEAN, is still grappling with a slowdown in export demand, particularly for coal and palm oil, while the rupiah has weakened against the dollar amid tightening global monetary conditions. The government’s fiscal stimulus package, announced in early 2024, has yet to translate into tangible growth acceleration, and the upcoming budget may face constraints as debt levels edge upward. These factors compound the anxiety that a MSCI downgrade could trigger a capital outflow at a time when the country needs foreign financing to support infrastructure projects and its ambitious renewable‑energy transition.

Nevertheless, some market participants see a silver lining. The steep decline has made Indonesian equities more attractive on a valuation basis, with price‑to‑earnings multiples now among the cheapest in the region. “If the downgrade does not materialise, we could see a rapid rebound as bargain hunters step in,” suggested Ahmad Faizal, head of research at Danareksa. Moreover, the Indonesian Stock Exchange is working on reforms to improve market depth, including the introduction of more derivatives contracts and a push for greater participation by institutional investors.

Looking ahead, the trajectory of Indonesia’s stock market will hinge on two pivotal developments: MSCI’s final verdict and the government’s ability to sustain fiscal support without jeopardising debt sustainability. Investors will be watching the MSCI decision, expected later this year, for any signals that could either restore confidence or cement the outflow trend. In the meantime, the market’s volatility may present opportunities for risk‑tolerant investors, but the underlying structural challenges underscore the need for continued reforms to ensure that Indonesia remains an appealing destination for long‑term foreign capital.
